question.text: In adults with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or elevated triglycerides (>500 mg/dL), does prescription EPA (icosapent ethyl) at 4 g/day reduce major adverse cardiovascular events compared with placebo?

support: EPA 4 g/day provides ~4 g of EPA (~2 % of total daily calories), contributing modestly to omega‑3 intake without displacing other macronutrients
High-dose EPA has been shown to modestly increase bleeding time, especially in patients on anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents (relevant red‑flag)
EPA supplementation does not supply significant micronutrients, so no risk of vitamin/mineral deficiency
concerns: Potential for increased bleeding risk in patients on anticoagulant therapy or with atrial fibrillation history
High EPA dose may cause gastrointestinal upset and rare elevations in serum triglycerides paradoxically
No contribution to essential nutrients; reliance on supplement could reduce intake of whole‑food omega‑3 sources
verdicts.notes: Overall nutritional profile is acceptable, but safety considerations (bleeding, GI tolerance) warrant a cautious recommendation pending clinical efficacy data.

support: EPA (eicosapentaenoic acid) at 4 g/day can modestly increase bleeding time, which may potentiate anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy (HDI class: coagulation)
No severe hepatotoxicity signals for EPA in LiverTox; mild, reversible elevations in liver enzymes have been reported only at very high doses
Renal clearance of EPA is not a concern; no known CYP450 or P‑gp interactions
Pregnancy: EPA is generally considered safe in moderate amounts, but high‑dose supplementation (>3 g/day) is not routinely recommended due to limited data
concerns: Potential additive bleeding risk when combined with warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants, or aspirin
Mild gastrointestinal upset (nausea, diarrhea) reported in a subset of users at high doses
Rare paradoxical rise in triglycerides in some individuals
Lack of robust data on long‑term safety of chronic high‑dose EPA supplementation
verdicts.notes: Given the modest increase in bleeding propensity and the absence of severe organ toxicity, EPA 4 g/day should be recommended with caution, especially in patients on anticoagulant or antiplatelet agents. Monitoring of coagulation parameters and gastrointestinal tolerance is advised.
All nutritional and safety considerations have been addressed by the Dietitian and SafetyReviewer. Clinical decision should be made by the treating physician.

support: EPA at 4 g/day may increase bleeding time, interacting with anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs (HDI class: coagulation)
LiverTox reports no severe hepatotoxicity for EPA; only mild, reversible enzyme elevations at very high doses
No documented CYP450, P‑gp, PD‑antagonism, or serotonergic interactions for EPA
concerns: Additive bleeding risk when combined with warfarin, DOACs, or aspirin
Possible gastrointestinal discomfort (nausea, diarrhea) at high doses
Limited data on safety of chronic high‑dose EPA in pregnancy and pediatric populations
verdicts.notes: Recommend EPA 4 g/day with caution. Monitor coagulation parameters in patients on anticoagulants/antiplatelets and assess GI tolerance. No contraindication to use, but heightened vigilance is warranted.
